formula: I(choice == "choice1") ~ 0 + I(price1 - price2) + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) + (0 + I(time1 - time2) + I(change1 - change2) + I(comfort1 - comfort2) | id)
notes: mlogit's vignette c5.mxl.qmd (read, cran/mlogit) fits mixed logits on mlogit's copy of this table (the same 2929 stated-preference choices of Meijer and Rouwendal, the attributes named price_A to comfort_B there): Train.mxlu <- mlogit(choice ~ price + time + change + comfort | - 1, Tr, panel = TRUE, rpar = c(time = "n", change = "n", comfort = "n"), R = 100, correlation = FALSE, halton = NA, method = "bhhh"), then Train.mxlc <- update(Train.mxlu, correlation = TRUE): correlated normal coefficients on time, change and comfort per individual (id), a fixed price coefficient and no alternative intercept (price rescaled to euros and time to hours there). With two alternatives the conditional logit is a logit of choosing choice1 on the attribute differences, so the formula renders the correlated model on I(x1 - x2). Meijer and Rouwendal (2006), cited by the help page, fit random-coefficient logits to these data. Hand check #162: the random part holds correlated normal slopes on the time, change and comfort differences, without a random intercept; the differences are no columns, so covariates list the eight attribute columns, random_slopes stays blank and the formula alone states the slopes. Train.mxlu's independent slopes have the same response and grouping, so they file no row. choiceid numbers an individual's choice tasks, ignored.

formula: Tuna.choice ~ brand intercepts + log(price.<brand>) (conditional logit over skw, cosw, sko, coso and pw) + a household-varying log-price coefficient (reflected lognormal) and a two-point oil-versus-water intercept shifter over Tuna.hid
notes: Kim, Blattberg and Rossi (1995), JBES 13(3), 291-303, cited by the help page, abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc: a random-coefficient logit in which brand-specific intercepts and price-slope coefficients vary across households, fitted to household panel data of two product categories, its parametric heterogeneity distribution checked against semiparametric density estimates. Tuna.hid the household, Tuna.id its purchase occasions (ignored), Tuna.choice the brand chosen among five (Starkist and Chicken of the Sea in water and oil, store label in water), price.<brand> each brand's price at the purchase. Hand check #162: the paper (equations 1 and 2) takes log prices, a reflected lognormal price coefficient and an independent two-point shifter of the oil-packed brands against the water-packed ones, not normal brand intercepts, as for Ketchup; a conditional logit is outside Family, so family stays blank, and the price coefficient acts on each brand's column, which random_slopes cannot name, so the formula states it in words. Table 4's fixed price slope, Table 12's two- to six-class mixtures and section 4.1's semiparametric densities have the same response and grouping, so they file no row. The paper's full specification was not read, hence medium.

formula: lnexp12m ~ lntotal + age + sex + hhsize + farm + educyr + (1 | commune)
notes: The help page cites Cameron and Trivedi (2005) pp. 88-90, the quantile regression of lnmed on lntotal in mma04p2qreg.do (qreg0902.dta: sex, age, educyr98, farm, urban98, hhsize, lhhexp1, lhhex12m, lnrlfood), with no commune term. The same book's section 24.7, pp. 848-53, Table 24.4, program mma24p1olscluster.do (read), takes the 5999 households of vietnam_ex1.dta in 194 communes and fits xtreg LNEXP12M LNHHEXP AGE SEX HHSIZE FARM EDUC, re and , mle after iis COMMUNE (random commune intercepts), beside OLS with cluster-robust errors and commune fixed effects. LNEXP12M is lnexp12m (lhhex12m) and LNHHEXP lntotal (lhhexp1); EDUC there is comped98 (completed diploma), which this table lacks, so educyr (years of schooling) stands in, hence medium. lnmed repeats lhhex12m under the quantile regression's name, ignored; urban and lnrlfood are not in the model. Hand check #162: published_model no: the program's EDUC is comped98, which the table lacks, so the formula with educyr standing in is the reader's adaptation of the published model; commune stands (194 communes of 16 to 40 households).

RESPONSE INFERRED: breaches of health records of 500 or more people reported to HHS by June 2014; the help page fits no model (its examples take quantiles of Individuals_Affected and of the breach lengths). Individuals_Affected (records compromised per breach, at least 500 by law, heavy-tailed) is the outcome a reader would model, log-transformed with a gaussian family; State (the 50 states, DC and Puerto Rico) groups the breaches, a reader's choice; the breach type, the location of the breached information (multi-valued text categories) and year as covariates. Ignored: Number (record id), Name_of_Covered_Entity (the entity's name), Business_Associate_Involved, Summary, Date_of_Breach with its recodes breach_start and breach_end, and Date_Posted_or_Updated. Hand check #162: State stands, an exhaustive set of many units (52 states and territories of 1 to 113 breaches); 62 of the 967 covered entities report several breaches (150 rows), 61 with varying counts, a weaker grouping.

formula: log(fare) ~ concen + ldist + I(ldist^2) + y98 + y99 + y00 + (1 | id)
notes: Help page (Notes): "This data set nicely illustrates the different estimates obtained when applying pooled OLS, random effects, and fixed effects." Used in Text pages 506-507 and 581. Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics, Ch. 14 computer exercise on AIRFARE (recalled, not read): log(fare) on year intercepts, concen, log(dist) and its square plus a route effect, estimated by pooled OLS, random effects and fixed effects; the row renders the random-effects fit with a random intercept on the route (id). Wooldridge's 2020 UK Stata Conference slides (Correlated Random Effects Methods for Panel Data, Sec. 4) fit the same panel by xtreg lfare concen y98 y99 y00, fe vce(cluster id) and by the Mundlak regression adding concenbar, ldist and the squared demeaned ldist. concen equals bmktshr (an alias, ignored), ldistsq is ldist^2 (written I(ldist^2)), lfare and lpassen are logs, and year is coded by y98, y99 and y00. Medium: the random-effects specification is recalled from the book. Hand check #162: stands; Imbens and Wooldridge's cemmap slides (p. 121) fit xtreg lfare concen ldist ldistsq y98 y99 y00, re on these 4,596 rows of 1,149 routes. Their correlated random effects fit (p. 144, concen's route mean added) has the same response and grouping, so it files no row.

formula: passen ~ log(fare) + concen + ldist + I(ldist^2) + y98 + y99 + y00 + (1 | id), gamma-distributed multiplicative route effect by id
notes: Hand check #162: model 2 from the outside check. Wooldridge's 2011 lecture (Grinnell, p. 39) fits xtpoisson passen lfare concen ldist ldistsq y98 y99 y00, re on this table: a Poisson model whose route effect multiplies the rate as a gamma variate, Stata's default, which lme4 cannot state, so the formula names it. passen is the average daily passenger count, integers 2 to 8,497; lfare is log(fare) and ldistsq ldist^2, ignored.

formula: ecolbs ~ ecoprc + regprc + faminc + hhsize + educ + age + (1 | state)
notes: Help page (Notes): the price pairs "were randomly determined" and "the main dependent variable, ecolbs, piles up at zero, estimating a linear model is still worthwhile"; the demand equation regresses ecolbs on both prices (Used in Text pages 201, 223, 266, 626-627; the faminc, hhsize, educ and age controls are recalled from Wooldridge's exercises, not read). The source fits OLS without grouping. Respondents of the telephone survey repeat within their home state (state, a two-letter code), rendered as a random intercept at low, as a cluster the source treats as independent (HISTORY, Reading rulings). reglbs is the quantity of regular apples, an alternate response; id is the respondent. Hand check #162: state stands, an exhaustive set of many units (48 states and DC of 1 to 66 respondents), though the source treats respondents as independent.
